items.text: Group health plans typically require a minimum share of eligible employees to enroll before a carrier will write the policy. An ICHRA has no such threshold - even one eligible employee is enough to offer it. honorbrook-insurance.com

One reason small employers get turned down for group coverage, or priced out of it, rarely comes up in the conversation: participation minimums.

Most group health carriers require a minimum share of eligible employees, often a majority, to actually enroll before they will write the group. Miss that threshold because your team is spread across working spouses, part-timers, or people who already have coverage elsewhere, and the group option can disappear entirely, regardless of how healthy your team is.

An ICHRA does not carry that requirement. You can set an allowance and offer it even if only one eligible employee chooses to use it. Nobody is turned away for low uptake, and you are not restructuring your offer every renewal because participation dipped below a line you do not control.

This is one of the more common reasons a small employer we talk to shifts to an ICHRA. It is not always about cost. Sometimes it is simply that the group market will not take them as they are.

Worth a conversation if participation has ever been the reason a group quote fell through.

Honorbrook Insurance, Tysons VA. honorbrook-insurance.com

Ever been turned down for group health coverage because not enough employees signed up? Most carriers require a minimum share of your team to participate before they'll write the group, and small or spread-out teams often can't hit it. An ICHRA has no participation minimum - even one employee using it is enough. We'll walk through how it fits your roster, at no charge.
